COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (Reuters) -- Humble woodcutter Mohammed Sultan Nafeek's teenage daughter moved to Saudi Arabia to work as a housemaid to support her family after they were displaced by the 2004 tsunami. Now she is on death row, and all he can do is pray. Razeena Mohammad (left) and Mohammad Sultan Nafeek, parents of Rizana Nafeek. Rizana, who was 17 when she started work in Saudi Arabia, was convicted of killing a 4-month-old baby boy in her care just two weeks into her job. Nafeek says the child died accidentally, choking on milk. His daughter was sentenced to beheading in a case rights groups say underlines the vulnerability of many of the 1.5 million Sri Lankans who work abroad -- nearly 400,000 of them in Saudi Arabia alone. "Our family was suffering hardship, and so our daughter volunteered to go and work abroad to send money home," Nafeek told Reuters by telephone from his modest home in Mutur in Sri Lanka's war-torn northeast. After the December 2004 tsunami forced them from their home, the family was displaced again by renewed civil war between the state and separatist Tamil Tiger rebels. Nafeek visited Saudi Arabia with Sri Lanka's deputy foreign minister this month in a bid to secure clemency and met with relations of the dead child's parents but came away empty handed. Under Saudi law, a pardon is the gift of the family of the victim, and so far the parents of the dead child have refused to meet either the family or Sri Lankan officials. "The cops told us: 'Go and pray to Allah. If you can get the forgiveness of the parents, your daughter will be free,' " he said. "So I am praying all the time." "If we had been able to meet the parents, we are sure they would have been willing to forgive our daughter after seeing our situation." The Sri Lankan government is investigating the agency that sent Rizana to work abroad when she was technically still a child but remains hopeful she will be pardoned or exonerated. "I am fairly confident," said Deputy Foreign Minister Hussein Bhaila. "We have spoken to tribal leaders of their particular tribe, we have spoken to area officials... It is they who will now have to speak (to the parents)." "His Excellency the President (Mahinda Rajapaksa) has been following this case very keenly. This is an exceptional case because of her tender age," he added. Rights groups accuse the government of failing to protect its expatriate workers -- one of the main sources of foreign-exchange revenues for the $23 billion economy -- with legal aid. They also decry Saudi Arabia's legal system. "This case raises many troubling questions about the treatment of children and foreigners in Saudi Arabia's criminal-justice system," Human Rights Watch said in a statement issued overnight. "International law prohibits the death penalty for crimes committed before the age of 18." Saudi Arabia executed four Sri Lankans convicted of armed robbery earlier this year, and did not inform Sri Lankan authorities beforehand. Sri Lanka reinstated its own death penalty in 2004 after the murder of a high court judge, but it has been dormant since 1976. There is no indication any of the dozens of convicted murderers, rapists and drug smugglers on death row in Sri Lanka and effectively serving life prison terms will actually be executed. “The cops told us: ‘Go and pray to Allah. If you can get the forgiveness of the parents, your daughter will be free,’” he said. “So I am praying all the time.”

COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (Reuters) — Mohammed Sultan Nafeek, a poor woodcutter, says his teenage daughter went to Saudi Arabia to work as a domestic servant so she could help provide for her family after the 2004 tsunami drove them from their home. She is now awaiting execution, and her father says prayer is the only thing left to him.

Razeena Mohammad and Mohammad Sultan Nafeek are the parents of Rizana Nafeek. Rizana was 17 when she began working in Saudi Arabia. Two weeks after starting the job, she was found guilty of killing a 4-month-old boy who had been in her care. Her father maintains the baby’s death was an accident and says the child choked on milk.

Rizana was sentenced to be beheaded. Human rights organizations say her case highlights the risks faced by many of the 1.5 million Sri Lankans employed overseas, including almost 400,000 working in Saudi Arabia.

“Our family was in difficulty, so our daughter offered to go abroad and earn money to send back home,” Nafeek told Reuters by phone from his simple house in Mutur, in Sri Lanka’s conflict-scarred northeast.

The family had already been uprooted by the December 2004 tsunami, and later they were displaced once more when fighting resumed between the Sri Lankan government and separatist Tamil Tiger rebels.

Earlier this month, Nafeek traveled to Saudi Arabia with Sri Lanka’s deputy foreign minister in an effort to obtain mercy for his daughter. He met relatives of the dead child’s parents, but the visit produced no result.

In Saudi Arabia, forgiveness must come from the victim’s family for a pardon to be granted. So far, the dead child’s parents have declined to meet either Rizana’s family or Sri Lankan officials.

“The police told us, ‘Go and pray to Allah. If you can obtain forgiveness from the parents, your daughter will be released,’” Nafeek said. “So I pray constantly.”

“If we had been able to meet the parents, we feel sure they would have forgiven our daughter once they saw our circumstances,” he added.

Sri Lanka’s government is looking into the recruitment agency that sent Rizana overseas, since she was legally still a minor at the time. Officials say they still hope she may receive a pardon or be cleared.

“I am fairly confident,” Deputy Foreign Minister Hussein Bhaila said. “We have spoken with tribal leaders from their tribe, and we have spoken with local officials. Now they will have to speak to the parents.”

He added that President Mahinda Rajapaksa had been paying close attention to the case. “This is an exceptional case because of her young age,” Bhaila said.

Rights groups say Sri Lanka has not done enough to provide legal protection for its citizens working abroad, even though overseas workers are a major source of foreign-exchange income for the country’s $23 billion economy. They have also criticized Saudi Arabia’s justice system.

Human Rights Watch said in a statement released overnight that the case “raises many troubling questions” about how Saudi Arabia’s criminal justice system treats children and foreigners. The group noted that international law forbids executing people for crimes committed when they were under 18.

Earlier this year, Saudi Arabia executed four Sri Lankans who had been convicted of armed robbery, without notifying Sri Lankan authorities in advance.

Sri Lanka restored the death penalty in 2004 after a High Court judge was murdered, but no executions have been carried out there since 1976. There is no sign that any of the dozens of people on death row in Sri Lanka—convicted murderers, rapists, and drug traffickers who are effectively serving life sentences—will actually be put to death.

COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (Reuters) - The family of a Sri Lankan housemaid sentenced to death in Saudi Arabia has appealed for her life to be spared, saying the teenager had travelled abroad to help relatives left destitute after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.

Rizana Nafeek, from the eastern district of Trincomalee, was convicted by a Saudi court over the death of an infant in her care while she was working as a domestic helper. Her family and rights groups say she was a minor when she left Sri Lanka and that she had no proper legal assistance during parts of the case.

Her father, Mohamed Nafeek, has pleaded with Saudi authorities and the dead child’s family to grant clemency.

“We are poor people. She went to Saudi Arabia to support us after we lost everything,” he told local media, appealing for mercy and saying his daughter had denied intentionally harming the child.

Sri Lankan officials said the government was pursuing diplomatic efforts to save Nafeek, including appeals through the Foreign Ministry, the Sri Lankan mission in Riyadh and contacts with Saudi authorities. Officials have also sought a pardon from the infant’s family, whose forgiveness could be decisive under Saudi Arabia’s legal system in some death penalty cases.

Nafeek’s case has drawn strong criticism from Human Rights Watch, which said Saudi Arabia should not execute someone who was allegedly under 18 at the time of the offence. The New York-based group has also questioned the fairness of the proceedings, citing concerns about translation, access to legal representation and the reliability of a confession it said Nafeek later retracted.

Sri Lanka, which sends hundreds of thousands of workers to the Middle East, depends heavily on remittances from migrant labourers, many of them women employed as domestic workers. Rights advocates say such workers are often vulnerable to abuse, isolation and unfair treatment in the courts.

Nafeek’s relatives said the family had been displaced by the tsunami that devastated Sri Lanka’s eastern coast, destroying homes and livelihoods. They said she had taken the job in Saudi Arabia in desperation, hoping to help rebuild the family’s life.

The case has prompted renewed calls in Sri Lanka for tighter regulation of labour recruitment agencies and stronger protections for migrant workers, particularly young women sent abroad for domestic service.

## Sri Lankan Domestic Worker Faces Death Sentence in Saudi Arabia, Prompting Appeals for Clemency

**COLOMBO/RIYADH —** The family of a Sri Lankan domestic worker sentenced to death in Saudi Arabia has appealed for urgent government intervention, as Sri Lankan officials and international human rights groups renewed calls for greater protection of migrant workers facing criminal prosecution in the Gulf kingdom.

The woman, a Sri Lankan national employed as a domestic worker in Saudi Arabia, was sentenced to death by a Saudi court in a case that has drawn growing concern in Colombo and among rights advocates. Details of the case remain limited, in part because Saudi court proceedings are often held behind closed doors and foreign domestic workers frequently lack consistent access to legal representation and translation.

Her family says they were devastated to learn of the sentence and are pleading for her life to be spared.

“My daughter went abroad only to earn money for the family,” her father said from the family’s village in Sri Lanka. **[INSERT VERIFIED QUOTE FROM FATHER: e.g., appeal for mercy, description of family hardship, request to Sri Lankan government.]** “We ask the authorities to bring her back alive.”

Sri Lanka’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it was aware of the case and was working through diplomatic channels to support the worker and seek relief from the sentence.

A ministry official said Sri Lankan diplomats in Riyadh and Jeddah were in contact with Saudi authorities and were exploring all available legal and diplomatic options. **[INSERT VERIFIED QUOTE FROM FOREIGN MINISTRY OFFICIAL.]**

“The government is providing consular assistance and is pursuing the matter at the highest possible level,” the official said, adding that Colombo would seek clemency if the judicial process allowed it.

### Case Highlights Risks for Migrant Domestic Workers

The case has renewed scrutiny of the treatment of migrant domestic workers in Saudi Arabia, where hundreds of thousands of women from Sri Lanka, the Philippines, Indonesia, Nepal, Ethiopia and other countries are employed in private homes.

Rights groups say such workers are especially vulnerable because they often live inside their employers’ homes, face restrictions on movement, and may have limited access to phones, lawyers, embassies or independent witnesses.

Human rights organizations have long criticized Saudi Arabia’s justice system, saying defendants in capital cases may be convicted after unfair trials, sometimes without adequate interpretation or legal counsel.

A spokesperson for a human rights group said the case raised serious concerns about due process. **[INSERT VERIFIED QUOTE FROM HUMAN RIGHTS GROUP, SUCH AS AMNESTY INTERNATIONAL OR HUMAN RIGHTS WATCH.]**

“No one should face execution after proceedings that fail to meet international fair-trial standards,” the spokesperson said. “Migrant domestic workers are among the least protected people in the region, and governments must do far more to ensure they receive legal assistance from the moment they are arrested.”

### Diplomatic Pressure and Possible Clemency

Sri Lankan officials are expected to seek a review of the sentence and may request a royal pardon, depending on the nature of the conviction and the stage of the appeals process.

In some Saudi capital cases, clemency can depend on the approval of victims’ families or on intervention by the Saudi monarch. However, outcomes vary significantly depending on the charge, the court ruling and the interpretation of Islamic law applied by judges.

Sri Lanka’s Bureau of Foreign Employment, which regulates overseas labor migration, said it was gathering information about the worker’s recruitment history and employment conditions.

A senior bureau official said authorities were trying to determine whether she had migrated through formal channels and whether her family had received proper updates about her legal situation. **[INSERT VERIFIED QUOTE FROM BUREAU OFFICIAL.]**

Sri Lanka sends large numbers of workers overseas each year, and remittances remain a major source of foreign exchange for the island nation. Many of those workers are women from low-income households who take jobs as housemaids in the Middle East to support children, parents and extended families.

### Family Pleads for Her Return

At the woman’s family home, relatives described the sentence as unbearable.

Her father said the family had depended on her income and had believed she would return after completing her contract. Instead, they are now waiting anxiously for updates from officials.

“We are poor people,” he said. **[INSERT VERIFIED QUOTE FROM FATHER.]** “We do not know the law in that country. We only ask that she be given a chance to live.”

Local community leaders have also urged the Sri Lankan government to intensify its efforts. Some have called for a temporary review of recruitment practices for domestic workers bound for countries where labor protections and legal safeguards are considered weak.

### Calls for Reform

Human rights groups say the case should not be treated as an isolated incident. They argue that sending countries such as Sri Lanka must improve pre-departure training, ensure workers have emergency contacts, and provide immediate legal aid when migrants are arrested abroad.

They also say Saudi Arabia should reform its labor and criminal justice systems, including ending the death penalty and ensuring all defendants have access to lawyers, interpreters and consular representatives.

“Domestic workers are often invisible until something goes terribly wrong,” said a regional labor-rights advocate. **[INSERT VERIFIED QUOTE FROM RIGHTS ADVOCATE.]** “This case shows the urgent need for both Saudi Arabia and labor-sending countries to protect women before they are trapped in abusive or dangerous situations.”

Saudi authorities have not publicly commented in detail on the case. The Saudi government has previously said its courts operate according to Islamic law and that defendants have the right to appeal.

For now, the woman’s family says it is waiting for word from Colombo and Riyadh, hoping diplomatic intervention can stop the execution.

“My only wish is to see my daughter alive again,” her father said. **[INSERT VERIFIED QUOTE.]**
